nodes.title: Relative Hurewicz theorem with trivial π₁-action
nodes.statement: Let (X, A, a₀) be a based pair of path-connected spaces (a based NDR pair in the sense of AT stage 8), (n − 1)-connected with n ≥ 2, such that π₁(A, a₀) acts trivially on π_n(X, A, a₀). Then π_n(X, A, a₀) is abelian, H_i(X, A; ℤ) = 0 for i < n, and the Hurewicz map π_n(X, A, a₀) → H_n(X, A; ℤ) is an isomorphism. A is not assumed simply connected.
hypotheses: π₁(A) acts trivially on π_n(X, A); (X, A) (n − 1)-connected; n ≥ 2.
proofSteps: Reduce to a CW pair by a CW model of (X, A) (AT stage 8 / stage 4 cellular approximation).

Hatcher's proof of Theorem 4.37 (pp. 371–373): Lemma 4.38 (π_n(W, X) is the free ℤ[π₁X]-module on the attached n-cells when π₁X ≅ π₁W, via the universal cover and the relative form of Hatcher Proposition 4.1, that a covering projection induces π_n(W̃, p⁻¹X) ≅ π_n(W, X) for n ≥ 2; tauceti:IsCoveringMap.homotopyGroupMulEquiv covers only absolute groups, so this is the packet gap 'Relative homotopy groups of coverings') identifies π′_n(X, A) with H_n(X, A); with trivial action π′_n = π_n, and for n = 2 trivial action makes π₂(X, A) abelian.
acceptance: A and X simply connected: the AT stage 8 relative Hurewicz theorem.
Used in Hatcher's proofs of Lemma 4.70 and Proposition 4.74 (H.3/principal-fibration-criterion, H.3/abelian-homology-whitehead).

sources.locator: §4.2, Theorem 4.37 and Lemma 4.38 with proof, printed pp. 371–373 (PDF 380–382)
sources.match: Hatcher's general relative Hurewicz theorem, used here in the trivial-action case where π′_n = π_n.

nodes.title: When an inclusion with Eilenberg–Mac Lane fibre is a principal fibration
nodes.statement: Let (X, A) be a CW pair with X and A connected such that the homotopy fibre of A ⊂ X is a K(π, n), n ≥ 1. There is a map k : X → K(π, n+1) whose homotopy fibre receives A by a weak homotopy equivalence compatible with A ⊂ X iff π₁(A) acts trivially on π_{n+1}(X, A) ≅ π.
hypotheses: (X, A) CW pair, X and A connected, hofib(A ⊂ X) ≃ K(π, n), n ≥ 1 (π abelian).
proofSteps: Necessity: in a fibration π₁ of the fibre acts trivially on π_*(E, F) (Hatcher p. 413).

Sufficiency: (X, A) is n-connected with only π_{n+1}(X, A) ≅ π nonzero; relative Hurewicz with trivial action (H.3/relative-hurewicz-trivial-action) gives π_{n+1}(X, A) ≅ H_{n+1}(X, A); absolute Hurewicz on the n-connected X/A gives π_{n+1}(X/A) ≅ H_{n+1}(X/A); attach cells of dimension ≥ n+3 to X/A to get K(π, n+1) and let k be X → X/A → K(π, n+1); the five lemma on the long exact sequences of (X, A) and of the fibration pair shows A → hofib(k) is a weak equivalence (Hatcher Lemma 4.70).
acceptance: A central extension A → S → P: BS → BP has fibre BA = K(A, 1) and S acts trivially on π₂(BP, BS) ≅ A, so BS ≃ hofib(BP → K(A, 2)) (used by H.3/plus-uce-fibration).
RP² ⊂ RP^∞-type examples with non-trivial action are not principal.

sources.match: Hatcher's Lemma 4.70; the proof builds B = K(π, n+1) from X/A.

nodes.title: The Postnikov tower converges
nodes.statement: For a sequence of fibrations ⋯ → X₂ → X₁ the map λ : π_i(lim X_n) → lim π_i(X_n) is surjective, and injective if the maps π_{i+1}(X_n) → π_{i+1}(X_{n−1}) are surjective for large n. Consequently, for a Postnikov tower of fibrations of a connected CW complex X, the map X → lim X_n is a weak homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: The maps X_n → X_{n−1} are (Hurewicz or Serre) fibrations; X connected CW.
proofSteps: Surjectivity and injectivity of λ by inductive use of homotopy lifting for (Sⁱ, s₀) and (D^{i+1}, Sⁱ) (Hatcher Prop. 4.67).

For a Postnikov tower π_i(X) → π_i(X_n) is an isomorphism for n ≥ i, so the composite π_i(X) → π_i(lim X_n) → lim π_i(X_n) is an isomorphism and the hypotheses of the first part hold (Hatcher Cor. 4.68).
acceptance: A tower with surjective maps on π_{i+1} has no lim¹ term.

sources.locator: §4.3, Proposition 4.67 and Corollary 4.68 with proofs, printed pp. 410–411 (PDF 419–420)
sources.match: Corollary 4.68 (OCR prints the limit symbol on a separate line).

nodes.title: Cohomology is represented by Eilenberg–Mac Lane spaces
nodes.statement: For a CW complex X, an abelian group G and n ≥ 1, the map T : ⟨X, K(G, n)⟩ → H^n(X; G), [f] ↦ f*(α), with α ∈ H^n(K(G, n); G) the fundamental class (corresponding to id_G under H^n(K(G,n); G) ≅ Hom(H_n K(G,n), G) ≅ Hom(G, G)), is a natural bijection, where ⟨−, −⟩ denotes based homotopy classes and H^n is singular cohomology (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 6). For n ≥ 2 (K(G, n) simply connected) based and free classes coincide (Hatcher p. 394); this is the form used by H.3/obstruction-lifting.
hypotheses: X a CW complex (or of CW homotopy type); n ≥ 1; G abelian.
proofSteps: The functors h^n(X) = ⟨X, K(G, n)⟩ form a reduced cohomology theory on based CW complexes (wedge axiom, exactness from cofibre sequences, suspension iso from ΩK(G, n+1) ≃ K(G, n)) (Hatcher Theorem 4.58, printed p. 397, applied to the Ω-spectrum K(G, n) ≃_w ΩK(G, n+1); proof of Theorem 4.57, p. 402).

A cohomology theory with the same coefficients as H̃^*(−; G) and a natural map is isomorphic to it (uniqueness of cohomology theories on CW complexes, Hatcher Theorem 4.59, printed p. 399, by cellular comparison with Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stages 4 and 6).
acceptance: ⟨X, K(ℤ, 1)⟩ = H¹(X; ℤ) = [X, S¹] (Hatcher §4.3, Exercise 2).
k-invariants of Postnikov towers are classes in H^{n+1}(X_{n−1}; π_n X).

sources.match: Hatcher's Theorem 4.57, proved via Theorem 4.59 on uniqueness of cohomology theories.

nodes.title: Postnikov towers of principal fibrations for abelian spaces
nodes.statement: Every connected CW complex X has a Postnikov tower ⋯ → X_n → X_{n−1} → ⋯ → X_1 with maps X → X_n inducing isomorphisms on π_i for i ≤ n, π_i(X_n) = 0 for i > n, X → lim X_n a weak homotopy equivalence (H.3/postnikov-limit-weak-equivalence), and X_n → X_{n−1} a fibration with fibre K(π_n X, n). The tower can be chosen with each X_n → X_{n−1} a principal fibration, i.e. the homotopy fibre of a map k_n : X_{n−1} → K(π_n X, n+1), iff π₁(X) acts trivially on π_n(X) for all n > 1 (in particular for abelian X). If X is abelian the tower extends by X₀ = point with X₁ → X₀ principal (X₁ ≃ ΩK(π₁X, 2)).
hypotheses: X connected CW complex.
proofSteps: Construct X_n by attaching cells to X to kill π_i for i > n (Hatcher Example 4.16) and convert the maps X_n → X_{n−1} into fibrations with fibre K(π_n X, n) (Hatcher §4.3, p. 410; H.2/mapping-path-space-fibration).

Principality: for n ≥ 2 the action of π₁(X) on π_n(X) is identified with the action of π₁(X_n) on π_{n+1}(X_{n−1}, X_n) (exact sequence of the pair), and H.3/principal-fibration-criterion applies (Hatcher proof of Theorem 4.69, pp. 413–414); conversely a principal fibration has trivial action. For abelian X, X₁ = K(π₁X, 1) ≃ ΩK(π₁X, 2) gives the extra principal stage X₁ → X₀ = ∗ (Hatcher p. 416).
acceptance: For X = K(G, 1) the tower is constant from n = 1.
For RP² the action is nontrivial and no tower of principal fibrations exists.

sources.match: Hatcher's Theorem 4.69, after the construction of Postnikov towers.

nodes.title: Obstructions to extending maps through a principal fibration
nodes.statement: Let X_n → X_{n−1} be the principal fibration pulled back from the path fibration over K = K(π_n X, n+1) along k_n, (W, A) a CW pair and W → X_{n−1} a map with a lift A → X_n. The map W ∪ CA → K determines ω_n ∈ H^{n+1}(W ∪ CA; π_n X) ≅ H^{n+1}(W, A; π_n X), and a lift W → X_n extending the given one on A exists iff ω_n = 0.
hypotheses: (W, A) a CW pair; the fibration principal (H.3/postnikov-principal-fibrations).
proofSteps: A lift W → X_n is a null-homotopy of W → X_{n−1} → K extending the given one on A, i.e. an extension of W ∪ CA → K over CW (pullback description of X_n).

Such an extension exists iff W ∪ CA → K is null-homotopic (homotopy extension for (CW, W ∪ CA), Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4), iff its class ω_n vanishes (H.3/cohomology-representability) (Hatcher Proposition 4.72).
acceptance: If H^{n+1}(W, A; π_n X) = 0 there is no obstruction at stage n.

sources.match: Hatcher's Proposition 4.72.

nodes.title: Extending maps into abelian spaces
nodes.statement: Let X be a connected CW complex that is abelian, and (W, A) a CW pair. If the relative cohomology groups H^{n+1}(W, A; π_n X) vanish for every n, then each map A → X extends over W.
hypotheses: X connected abelian CW complex; (W, A) a CW pair.
proofSteps: Lift inductively through the principal Postnikov tower (H.3/postnikov-principal-fibrations), the obstructions vanishing by hypothesis (H.3/obstruction-lifting).

Pass to W → lim X_n and compress to X using the weak equivalence X → lim X_n (H.3/postnikov-limit-weak-equivalence) and the compression lemma (Hatcher Lemma 4.6, Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8), as in the paragraph before Corollary 4.73.
acceptance: Used with W the mapping cylinder of a homology isomorphism to build a retraction (H.3/abelian-homology-whitehead).

sources.match: Hatcher's Corollary 4.73.

nodes.title: Homology Whitehead theorem for abelian spaces
nodes.statement: If X and Y are connected abelian CW complexes and f : X → Y induces isomorphisms on all integral homology groups, then f is a homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: X, Y connected abelian CW complexes (or of CW homotopy type).
proofSteps: Replace f by the inclusion of a subcomplex via the mapping cylinder (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4).

H_*(Y, X) = 0 gives H^{n+1}(Y, X; π_n X) = 0 by universal coefficients (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 6), so the identity of X extends to a retraction Y → X (H.3/abelian-extension-corollary); hence π_n(Y) → π_n(Y, X) is onto and π₁(X) acts trivially on π_n(Y, X).

Relative Hurewicz with trivial π₁-action (H.3/relative-hurewicz-trivial-action; AT stage 8 has only the simply connected case) gives π_n(Y, X) = 0 for all n, so f is a weak equivalence and by Whitehead a homotopy equivalence (Hatcher Proposition 4.74).
acceptance: Simply connected case: Hatcher Corollary 4.33.

The abelian hypothesis cannot be dropped: Hatcher Example 4.35 (printed p. 368): X = (S¹ ∨ Sⁿ) ∪ e^{n+1} attached along 2t − 1 ∈ ℤ[t, t⁻¹] = π_n(S¹ ∨ Sⁿ); S¹ ⊂ X is a homology and π₁-isomorphism with π_n(X) ≅ ℤ[1/2], because π₁ acts nontrivially on π_n.

sources.match: Hatcher's Proposition 4.74.

planet.name: Homology Whitehead theorem for abelian spaces

nodes.title: Homology isomorphisms between H-spaces are homotopy equivalences
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be path-connected H-spaces of CW homotopy type and f : X → Y a map inducing an isomorphism H_*(X; ℤ) ≅ H_*(Y; ℤ). Then f is a homotopy equivalence. (f need not be an H-map.)
hypotheses: X, Y path-connected H-spaces with the homotopy type of CW complexes.
proofSteps: H-spaces are abelian (H.3/hspace-is-abelian); apply H.3/abelian-homology-whitehead after CW replacement.
Weibel's hint (trivial action of π₁(Y) on the homotopy fibre by [Wh, IV.3.6] and relative Hurewicz) is replaced by this route.
acceptance: BGL(R)⁺ ≃ H whenever BGL(R) → H is an integral homology isomorphism into an H-space (H.3/plus-hspace-recognition).

sources.match: Weibel's 'standard result' of Exercise 1.3, proved here from Hatcher 4A.3 and 4.74.

nodes.title: Universal property of the plus construction
nodes.statement: Let f : X → Y be a plus construction relative to P of connected CW complexes and g : X → Z a map to a connected abelian CW complex (for instance a connected H-space, H.3/hspace-is-abelian). Then P ⊆ ker(π₁ g) automatically (P is perfect and π₁Z abelian), there is h : Y → Z with h ∘ f ≃ g, and any two such h are freely homotopic; hence the maps h_* on homotopy groups are independent of h. The general case of Weibel IV Theorem 1.5(2) (arbitrary Z) is the packet gap 'Plus-construction universal property for non-abelian targets'.
hypotheses: X, Y connected CW complexes (or of CW homotopy type); Z a connected abelian CW complex.
Uniqueness is up to free homotopy, never literal equality of maps; for abelian Z free and based effects on π_* agree.
proofSteps: Make f cellular and replace it by the inclusion X ⊆ M_f of its mapping cylinder (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4: cellular approximation, mapping cylinders; M_f ≃ Y rel X). Since f is acyclic it is an integral homology isomorphism (H.3/acyclic-map-homology-criterion with M = ℤ), so H_*(M_f, X; ℤ) = 0 (Hatcher §4.3 Exercise 23, hint).

Existence: the obstruction groups H^{n+1}(M_f, X; π_n Z) vanish by universal coefficients (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 6); extend g over M_f by H.3/abelian-extension-corollary. Uniqueness: apply the same to (M_f × I, M_f × ∂I ∪ X × I), whose relative homology also vanishes.

The non-abelian case is not proved here. A route without twisted obstruction theory (packet-authored, not used): with W = Z ∪_X M_f, van Kampen gives π₁Z ≅ π₁W because g kills P, excision with local coefficients and H.3/acyclic-map-homology-criterion show Z → W is acyclic, so it is a homotopy equivalence by H.3/acyclic-pi1-iso-weak-equivalence.
acceptance: Functoriality of BGL(R)⁺ in R holds only up to homotopy and follows from (2) (Weibel IV 1.1.2).
Lemma 4.4.1 (group completion of group-like H-spaces) uses this with abelian targets.
Do not replace (2) by an assumed structure field.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.5 and the paragraph before it, p. IV.5
sources.match: Shows the universal property is stated with an external proof reference; the abelian-target proof is from Hatcher.
Hatcher's uniqueness for abelian targets, proved from Corollary 4.73.

planet.name: Universal property of the plus construction

nodes.title: Uniqueness of the plus construction up to homotopy under X
nodes.statement: If f : X → Y and f′ : X → Y′ are plus constructions relative to P of connected CW complexes and Y′ is abelian (for instance an H-space or simply connected), then the map h : Y → Y′ with h ∘ f ≃ f′ given by H.3/plus-construction-universal-property is a homotopy equivalence. Thus X⁺_P is well defined up to homotopy equivalence under X whenever one model is abelian, but different choices are not equal.
hypotheses: X, Y, Y′ connected CW complexes; Y′ abelian; P perfect normal.
proofSteps: H.3/plus-construction-universal-property gives h : Y → Y′ with h ∘ f ≃ f′.
h is acyclic: for every π₁(Y′)-module M, f and f′ induce isomorphisms on H_*(−; M), hence so does h (H.3/acyclic-map-homology-criterion, both directions).
h induces π₁Y ≅ π₁X/P ≅ π₁Y′, so h is a weak equivalence (H.3/acyclic-pi1-iso-weak-equivalence) and a homotopy equivalence by Whitehead (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8).
acceptance: Any two models of BGL(R)⁺ are homotopy equivalent (Weibel IV Definition 1.1 remark).

sources.match: Weibel's part (3), stated as a consequence of (2).

nodes.title: Functoriality of the plus construction up to homotopy
nodes.statement: Let φ : X → X′ be a map of connected CW complexes and P ⊆ π₁(X), P′ ⊆ π₁(X′) perfect normal subgroups with φ_*(P) ⊆ P′, and X′⁺_{P′} abelian (for instance BGL(R′)⁺, an H-space). Then there is φ⁺ : X⁺_P → X′⁺_{P′}, unique up to homotopy, with φ⁺ ∘ f ≃ f′ ∘ φ; (ψ ∘ φ)⁺ ≃ ψ⁺ ∘ φ⁺ when X″⁺ is abelian, and id⁺ ≃ id. The homotopies are free, so the maps on π₁ commute with the quotient isomorphisms of H.3/plus-construction-predicate only up to conjugation by the track of the base point; for abelian targets there is no ambiguity. Strictly functorial models exist (Weibel IV Constructions 1.9) but the statements here are only up to homotopy.
hypotheses: φ carries the selected perfect subgroup into the selected one; X, X′ connected CW complexes; X′⁺_{P′} abelian.
proofSteps: Apply H.3/plus-construction-universal-property to f′ ∘ φ : X → X′⁺, which kills P since φ_*(P) ⊆ P′ = ker(π₁ f′).
Composition and identities follow from uniqueness up to homotopy.
acceptance: Ring maps R → R′ induce BGL(R)⁺ → BGL(R′)⁺, unique up to homotopy (Weibel IV 1.1.2); for P = E(R) the condition holds because ring maps preserve elementary matrices.

sources.match: Weibel's functoriality up to homotopy, derived from Theorem 1.5.

nodes.title: Recognising plus constructions into H-spaces
nodes.statement: Let X be a connected CW complex whose fundamental group has perfect commutator subgroup P = [π₁X, π₁X] (for example X = BGL(R), P = E(R)), and let g : X → H be a map to a path-connected H-space of CW homotopy type. Then g factors up to homotopy through X → X⁺_P by a map g⁺ whose effect on homotopy groups is independent of the factorisation; if moreover X⁺_P is abelian (for instance an H-space, as BGL(R)⁺ is by Weibel IV Exercise 1.11) and g induces an isomorphism H_*(X; ℤ) ≅ H_*(H; ℤ), then g is acyclic and g⁺ : X⁺_P → H is a homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: H a path-connected H-space of CW homotopy type; X⁺_P must be abelian for the last clause; an H-space structure is a sufficient condition (as for BGL(R)⁺).
proofSteps: π₁(H) is abelian (H.3/hspace-is-abelian), so P = [π₁X, π₁X] maps trivially; H is abelian, so H.3/plus-construction-universal-property (abelian-target case) gives g⁺, unique up to homotopy, which fixes its effect on π_* (Weibel IV Theorem 1.8).

If g is an integral homology isomorphism, so is g⁺ (H.3/plus-integral-homology); X⁺_P and H are abelian, so g⁺ is a homotopy equivalence (H.3/abelian-homology-whitehead); then g ≃ g⁺ ∘ f is acyclic (homotopy fibres are invariant under homotopy, H.2/homotopy-fibre-transport, and under composition with a homotopy equivalence) (Weibel IV Remark 1.8.1, Exercise 1.3).
acceptance: BGL(F_q)⁺ ≃ the homotopy fibre of ψ^q − 1 on BU, by applying the recognition to Quillen's Brauer-lift map (Weibel IV Theorem 1.12, the use in KTheoryFiniteLocalFields:L.1).
Z × BGL(R)⁺ ≃ the group completion of ⊔ BGL_n(R) (H.4/gl-telescope-plus-comparison).

sources.match: Weibel's Theorem 1.8 (proof omitted, citing Gersten) and Remark 1.8.1 (proof indicated in Exercise 1.3), proved here from the abelian obstruction theory.

uses.how: BGL(F_q)⁺ ≃ FΨ^q from an integral homology isomorphism into an H-space (the consumer cites H.3/plus-construction-universal-property for this)

nodes.title: π₂ of a plus construction and universal central extensions
nodes.statement: Let P be a perfect normal subgroup of a group G and f : BG → (BG)⁺_P the plus construction killing P, with homotopy fibre F(f) based over the image of the canonical vertex. The induced fundamental group of (BG)⁺_P is G/P, and the composite π₁(F(f)) → G factors through a surjective central extension of P that is universal. Its kernel is π₂((BG)⁺_P), naturally identified with H₂(P;ℤ). For G = GL(R) and P = E(R), this gives π₂BGL(R)⁺ ≅ H₂(E(R);ℤ), the Steinberg-extension kernel.
hypotheses: P perfect normal in G; the recognition theorem for universal central extensions (a central extension X of a perfect group is universal iff H₁(X) = H₂(X) = 0, with kernel H₂(P) by Hopf's formula) is the node K2SymbolsBrauer:T.1/recognition-theorem with the kernel computation K2SymbolsBrauer:T.1:classical/uce-kernel-h2.
proofSteps: Transport P to a subgroup of π₁(BG) along the canonical multiplicative equivalence π₁(BG) ≃* G. The quotient comparison for plus gives π₁((BG)⁺_P) ≃* G/P and identifies the induced map with the quotient map. Since π₂(BG)=0, the homotopy sequence identifies π₂((BG)⁺_P) with the kernel of the resulting surjection π₁F(f) → P.

π₂(BG⁺) is central in π₁F(f): the image of π₂(B) → π₁(F) of a fibre sequence is central (H.2/fibre-sequence-low-degree in its general form: ∂ is equivariant for the conjugation action of π₁(F) and the action of π₁(F) on π₂(BG⁺), which is trivial because F → BG⁺ is null; Hatcher printed p. 413; [Wh, IV.3.5]).
F(f) is acyclic, so π₁F(f) is perfect with H₂ = 0 (H.3/acyclic-space-perfect-fundamental-group).
The recognition theorem (K2SymbolsBrauer:T.1/recognition-theorem) identifies π₁F(f) as the universal central extension of P, whose kernel is H₂(P; ℤ) (Weibel IV Proposition 1.7).
acceptance: K₂(R) = π₂BGL(R)⁺ ≅ H₂(E(R); ℤ) (Weibel IV Corollary 1.7.1).
For P = G perfect, π₂(BG⁺) ≅ H₂(G; ℤ) agrees with Hurewicz on the simply connected BG⁺.
Naturality in R is H.3/plus-pi2-natural (the plus construction is only homotopy functorial).

For P = {1} in any G, including a nonperfect G such as the cyclic group of order two, π₁((BG)⁺_P) ≃* G and π₂((BG)⁺_P) is trivial. This checks that the contract depends on P rather than assuming G itself perfect.

sources.match: Proposition 1.7 applies to any perfect normal subgroup, with the extension map landing in that subgroup. Its proof uses the fibre homotopy sequence, acyclicity and recognition of universal central extensions; Corollary 1.7.1 specialises to stable elementary groups.

api.statement: For arbitrary P perfect normal in G, an equivalence π₂((BG)⁺_P) ≃* Multiplicative H₂(P;ℤ), using trivial coefficients. The coefficient ring and module are the universe lift of ℤ required by P; P=G is only a special case.

api.name: TauCeti.plusConstruction.fiber_universalCentralExtension
api.statement: For F the based homotopy fibre of BG → (BG)⁺_P, a surjection π₁F → P with central kernel, whose composite with P → G is induced by F → BG, and which admits a unique lift to every surjective central extension of P. This expresses the supplier-owned universal-central-extension property rather than introducing another definition.

nodes.title: Naturality of π₂(BG⁺) ≅ H₂(P; ℤ)
nodes.statement: Let φ : G → G′ be a homomorphism with φ(P) ⊆ P′ for perfect normal subgroups P ⊆ G, P′ ⊆ G′, f : BG → BG⁺ and f′ : BG′ → BG′⁺ plus constructions relative to P and P′, and φ⁺ : BG⁺ → BG′⁺ with a homotopy H : φ⁺ ∘ f ≃ f′ ∘ Bφ (H.3/plus-construction-functoriality). Assume either that H is based or that π₁(BG′⁺) acts trivially on π₂(BG′⁺) (e.g. BG′⁺ an H-space). Then under the isomorphisms π₂(BG⁺) ≅ H₂(P; ℤ) and π₂(BG′⁺) ≅ H₂(P′; ℤ) of H.3/plus-pi2-universal-central-extension, φ⁺_* corresponds to H₂(φ|_P; ℤ).
hypotheses: φ(P) ⊆ P′; H based, or trivial π₁-action on π₂ of the target.
proofSteps: H induces a map of homotopy fibres F(f) → F(f′) compatible with the long exact sequences (H.2/homotopy-fibre-transport, H.2/long-exact-sequence).

On π₁ it is a homomorphism of central extensions π₁F(f) → π₁F(f′) over φ|_P : P → P′; by uniqueness of lifts between universal central extensions (K2SymbolsBrauer:T.1:classical/uce-lift) it is the lift, so on kernels it is H₂(φ|_P; ℤ) (K2SymbolsBrauer:T.1:classical/uce-kernel-h2-natural).
The kernels are π₂(BG⁺) and π₂(BG′⁺) via ∂, and ∂ is natural; with a free homotopy the comparison holds up to the π₁(BG′⁺)-action, trivial by hypothesis.
acceptance: For a ring map R → R′, K₂(R) → K₂(R′) corresponds to H₂(E(R)) → H₂(E(R′)) (requested by K3BlochGroups V.1).

sources.locator: Proposition 1.7 with proof and Corollary 1.7.1, p. IV.6
sources.match: The identification whose naturality is proved; the naturality itself is packet-authored, as requested by K3BlochGroups V.1.

nodes.title: BP⁺ is the universal cover of BG⁺
nodes.statement: Let P ⊆ H ⊆ G with P perfect and normal in G, and f : BG → BG⁺ a plus construction relative to P. The covering of BG⁺ with group H/P ⊆ G/P, pulled back along f, is a plus construction of BH (≃ the covering of BG with group H) relative to P; hence BH⁺_P is homotopy equivalent to that covering, compatibly with the maps from BH, and π_n(BH⁺_P) ≅ π_n(BG⁺) for n ≥ 2. For H = P this says BP⁺ is the universal cover of BG⁺. For G = GL(R), P = E(R): BE(R)⁺ is the universal cover of BGL(R)⁺ and K_n(R) ≅ π_n BE(R)⁺ for n ≥ 2; for a commutative ring and H = SL(R) = ker(det : GL(R) → R^×) (E(R) ⊆ SL(R), and SL(R)/E(R) ⊆ GL(R)/E(R) is abelian by KTheoryLowDegrees:U.1/whitehead-lemma, so E(R) is the perfect radical of SL(R)), BSL(R)⁺ → BGL(R)⁺ is an isomorphism on π_n for n ≥ 2.
hypotheses: P ⊆ H ⊆ G, P perfect and normal in G.
proofSteps: BH is homotopy equivalent to the covering space of BG with group H (H.1/translation-category-classifying-space, X = G/H); it is the pullback along f of the covering of BG⁺ with group H/P (Weibel IV Exercise 1.8 hint).

The map BH → the covering of BG⁺ is the pullback of f along that covering; its homotopy fibres are those of f, so it is acyclic, and its kernel on π₁ is P. When H = P, both plus targets are simply connected and H.3/plus-construction-uniqueness applies. For general H/P, abelianness of BH⁺_P is not assumed: the equivalence under BH requires the general relative uniqueness statement recorded in the non-abelian-target gap.
Covering maps induce isomorphisms on π_n for n ≥ 2 (Tau Ceti IsCoveringMap.homotopyGroupMulEquiv).
acceptance: π₁(BE(R)⁺) = 0 and π₂(BE(R)⁺) ≅ K₂(R).
For P = G this is the identity.

sources.match: Weibel's exercise and its GL/E and SL applications; the proof steps are packet-authored from the hint.

nodes.title: The plus-construction fibration of a universal central extension
nodes.statement: If A → S → P is a universal central extension (S and P perfect), there is a homotopy fibre sequence BA → BS⁺ → BP⁺. Consequently π_n(BS⁺) = 0 for n ≤ 2, π_n(BS⁺) ≅ π_n(BP⁺) for n ≥ 3, and π₃(BP⁺) ≅ H₃(S; ℤ) by Hurewicz. For S = St(R), P = E(R): K_n(R) ≅ π_n BSt(R)⁺ for n ≥ 3 and K₃(R) ≅ H₃(St(R); ℤ).
hypotheses: A → S → P universal central extension; plus constructions relative to the whole perfect groups.
proofSteps: BA → BS → BP is a fibre sequence (H.2/group-extension-fibration). Since A is central, π₁(BS) = S acts trivially on π₂(BP, BS) ≅ π₁(BA) = A, so BS → BP is, up to weak equivalence, the homotopy fibre of a map k : BP → K(A, 2) (H.3/principal-fibration-criterion, n = 1).

K(A, 2) is simply connected, so k factors through BP⁺ (H.3/plus-construction-universal-property). With F′ the homotopy fibre of BP⁺ → K(A, 2), H.3/plus-relative-fibre-comparison over the simply connected base K(A, 2) (E = BP, F = BS) shows BS → F′ is an integral homology isomorphism.

π₁(F′) is a quotient of π₂K(A, 2) = A, hence abelian, and H₁(F′) = H₁(S) = 0, so F′ is simply connected; BS → F′ is then acyclic with kernel S (H.3/acyclic-map-homology-criterion, π₁ = 0 case) and F′ ≃ BS⁺ (H.3/plus-construction-uniqueness). Rotating BS⁺ → BP⁺ → K(A, 2) gives BA ≃ ΩK(A, 2) → BS⁺ → BP⁺ (H.3/eilenberg-maclane-space).

S and P are perfect and H₂(S; ℤ) = 0 (K2SymbolsBrauer:T.1/uce-perfect, K2SymbolsBrauer:T.1:classical/uce-source-superperfect), so π₁(BS⁺) = 0 and π₂(BS⁺) ≅ H₂(S) = 0; Hurewicz (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8) gives π₃(BS⁺) ≅ H₃(S), and the long exact sequence identifies π_n(BP⁺) for n ≥ 3 (Weibel IV Exercise 1.9).
acceptance: K₃(R) ≅ H₃(St(R); ℤ) (the use in K3BlochGroups:V.1/k3-h3-steinberg).
For the trivial extension of a perfect group with H₂ = 0, BA is a point.

sources.match: Weibel's exercise and its Steinberg application.

nodes.title: Plus constructions of fibre sequences
nodes.statement: Let F → E →p B be a homotopy fibre sequence of connected CW complexes with B simply connected, P ⊆ π₁(E) a perfect normal subgroup, f : E → E⁺ a plus construction relative to P and p⁺ : E⁺ → B with p⁺ ∘ f ≃ p (H.3/plus-construction-universal-property; B is abelian). Let F′ be the homotopy fibre of p⁺ and F → F′ the map induced by f and the homotopy. Then F → F′ is an integral homology isomorphism. If F′ is simply connected, F → F′ is acyclic with kernel π₁(F) (which is therefore perfect), so F′ ≃ F⁺ under F and F⁺ → E⁺ → B is a homotopy fibre sequence. If F′ is only abelian and F → F⁺ is a plus construction relative to Q = ker(π₁F → π₁F′) with F⁺ abelian, then F⁺ ≃ F′ under F.
hypotheses: B simply connected, so both Serre spectral sequences have constant coefficients; all spaces connected CW complexes.
proofSteps: Compare the Serre spectral sequences of F → E → B and F′ → E⁺ → B over the identity of B (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 5); since E → E⁺ is an integral homology isomorphism, H.3/serre-comparison-fibre gives that F → F′ is one.

If F′ is simply connected, F → F′ is acyclic (H.3/acyclic-map-homology-criterion, π₁ = 0 case) with kernel π₁F, hence a plus construction, and F′ ≃ F⁺ (H.3/plus-construction-uniqueness). If F′ is abelian, the universal property gives F⁺ → F′ under F, an integral homology isomorphism of abelian spaces, hence a homotopy equivalence (H.3/abelian-homology-whitehead).

No source read states the general relative plus construction; the form here is packet-authored around Weibel IV Exercise 1.9 and the roadmap's requirement ('Include the relative construction needed to compare fibres after applying plus'); recorded in the gap 'Relative plus construction'.
acceptance: The universal central extension case BA → BS⁺ → BP⁺ (H.3/plus-uce-fibration).
For a product E = F × B with P ⊆ π₁F the conclusion is (F × B)⁺ ≃ F⁺ × B (Weibel IV Exercise 1.7 for products of groups).

sources.match: The model case of the relative comparison; the general statement is packet-authored.

nodes.title: Serre classes in fibrations with trivial action
nodes.statement: Let C be one of FG (finitely generated abelian groups), T_P (P-torsion) or F_P (finite P-torsion). Let F → X → B be a fibration of path-connected spaces with π₁(B) acting trivially on H_*(F; ℤ). If H_n(F; ℤ) and H_n(B; ℤ) lie in C for all n > 0, so does H_n(X; ℤ); if H_n(F; ℤ) and H_n(X; ℤ) lie in C for all n > 0, so does H_n(B; ℤ).
hypotheses: Trivial monodromy on H_*(F; ℤ); C closed under subgroups, quotients, extensions, ⊗ and Tor (SSAT properties (1), (2)).
proofSteps: Case 1: the natural universal coefficient short exact sequence has left term H_p(B) ⊗ H_q(F), middle term E²_{p,q}, and right term Tor(H_{p−1}(B), H_q(F)); closure under extensions puts E²_{p,q} in C for (p, q) ≠ (0, 0) (untwisted E² page, AT stage 5); by induction on r the pages stay in C, and H_n(X) is filtered with quotients E^∞_{p, n−p} ∈ C.
Case 2: induction on k using the exact sequences 0 → E^{r+1}_{k,0} → E^r_{k,0} → im d_r → 0 (Hatcher SSAT, proof of Lemma 1.9).
acceptance: A product fibration F × B → B satisfies the hypothesis.
Without trivial action the lemma fails: S¹ ∨ S² has finitely generated homology but its universal cover does not (SSAT p. 14).

sources.match: Cases 1 and 2 of the lemma (SSAT omits case 3, which is not needed).

nodes.title: Homology of Eilenberg–Mac Lane spaces lies in the Serre class
nodes.statement: For C one of FG, T_P, F_P and π ∈ C, H_k(K(π, n); ℤ) ∈ C for all k, n > 0.
hypotheses: π abelian in C; n ≥ 1.
proofSteps: Reduce to n = 1 by the path fibration K(π, n−1) → P → K(π, n) (base simply connected for n ≥ 2) and H.3/serre-class-fibration.

n = 1, C = FG or F_P: π is a finite product of cyclic groups; K(G₁ × G₂, 1) = K(G₁, 1) × K(G₂, 1) (Künneth, AT stage 5, or H.3/serre-class-fibration for the product fibration); K(ℤ, 1) ≃ S¹; H_k(K(ℤ/m, 1); ℤ) = H_k(ℤ/m; ℤ) is ℤ/m for odd k and 0 for even k > 0 (H.1/bar-complex-comparison with Mathlib's finite cyclic group homology).
n = 1, C = T_P: π is the filtered union of its finitely generated subgroups G, and H_k(Bπ) = colim H_k(BG) (H.1/filtered-colimit-homology), each in F_P.
acceptance: H_k(K(ℤ/2, 1); ℤ) = H_k(RP^∞; ℤ) is ℤ/2 for odd k, 0 for even k > 0.

sources.match: Statement and the reduction to n = 1; the cyclic case uses group homology in place of lens spaces.

nodes.title: Serre class theory for abelian spaces
nodes.statement: Let C be one of: finitely generated abelian groups, P-torsion groups, finite P-torsion groups. For a path-connected abelian space X (in particular a connected H-space, such as BGL(R)⁺ or a component of the K-theory space), π_n(X) ∈ C for all n ≥ 1 iff H_n(X; ℤ) ∈ C for all n > 0; and if π_i(X) ∈ C for i < n then the Hurewicz map π_n(X) → H_n(X) is an isomorphism modulo C.
hypotheses: X path-connected and abelian (trivial π₁-action on all π_n, n ≥ 1).
proofSteps: Simply connected case: for the Postnikov tower of X, H_i(X_n) ∈ C for i > 0 by induction on n (H.3/serre-class-fibration, H.3/serre-class-eilenberg-maclane), and H_i(X) ≅ H_i(X_n) for i ≤ n because X_n is X with cells of dimension ≥ n + 2 attached (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4) (Hatcher SSAT proof of 1.7 and 1.8, p. 16).

Mod-C Hurewicz: the five-term sequence of F_n → X_n → X_{n−1} (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 5) shows H_n(F_n) → H_n(X_n) is an isomorphism mod C, and Hurewicz for the (n−1)-connected F_n = K(π_n X, n) (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8) gives Theorem 1.8.

Abelian case: use the tower of principal fibrations (H.3/postnikov-principal-fibrations); in a principal fibration π₁ of the base acts trivially on the homology of the fibre, since the transport maps K(π, n) → K(π, n) are homotopic to the identity (SSAT p. 38). Theorem 1.7 follows by applying 1.8 to the stages.
acceptance: S¹ ∨ S² is not abelian and has π₂ not finitely generated although its homology is (SSAT p. 14): the abelian hypothesis is needed.
If H_*(BGL(R)⁺) is finitely generated in each degree then K_n(R) is finitely generated for n ≥ 1 (the use in ArithmeticKTheory:N.3:finite-generation/quillen-finiteness-criterion).

The same reduction for hermitian K-theory (Calmès et al. Remark 2.3.20): for a number ring O the groups GW^q_n(O; ε) are finitely generated as soon as the integral homology of the components of Ω^∞GW^q(O; ε), which are connected H-spaces, is finitely generated in each degree.

sources.match: Hatcher's Theorem 1.7 for abelian spaces and the mod-C Hurewicz Theorem 1.8.
The first step of the remark is this theorem applied to the components, which are connected H-spaces.

nodes.title: Rational homotopy of H-spaces (Cartan–Serre)
nodes.statement: Let X be a path-connected H-space of CW homotopy type with H_n(X; ℚ) finite-dimensional for each n. Then H*(X; ℚ) is a free graded-commutative algebra (polynomial on even and exterior on odd generators) and X_ℚ is a product of Eilenberg–Mac Lane spaces K(ℚ, n_i); π_*(X) ⊗ ℚ has a basis in bijection with the free generators, and the rational Hurewicz map π_n(X) ⊗ ℚ → H_n(X; ℚ) is injective with image the primitive elements of the Hopf algebra H_*(X; ℚ).
hypotheses: X path-connected H-space (hence abelian, H.3/hspace-is-abelian), finite type rational homology. The degree-one factor π₁(X) ⊗ ℚ is included (π₁ abelian).
proofSteps: Hopf–Borel: H*(X; ℚ) is a commutative, associative Hopf algebra of finite type (Künneth, Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 5; cup products, stage 6), hence free graded-commutative (Hatcher AT Theorem 3C.4, printed p. 285).

Cartan–Serre: the product f : X → ∏ K(ℚ, n_i) of the maps given by the generators is a rational homology isomorphism, hence the ℚ-localisation of the abelian space X (SSAT Theorem 1.23, pp. 35–38, P = ∅), using H*(K(ℚ, n); ℚ) = ℚ[x] or Λ[x] (SSAT Proposition 1.20, p. 31, proved with the multiplicative cohomology Serre spectral sequence: packet gap 'Cohomology Serre spectral sequence with products'); so π_*(X) ⊗ ℚ has the stated basis (SSAT Theorem 1.24).

Primitives: Hurewicz images are primitive for the diagonal coproduct (Δ_*[Sⁿ] = [Sⁿ] ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ [Sⁿ]); rational Hurewicz is injective because along f it becomes the Hurewicz map of a product of K(ℚ, n)'s, injective factor by factor (Hurewicz in the first nonzero degree, Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8 and H.3/hurewicz-degree-one); and dim π_n(X) ⊗ ℚ = number of degree-n generators = dim (QH*)_n = dim Prim(H_*)_n by finite-type duality. Hence the image is exactly the primitives; Milnor–Moore is not needed (packet-authored).
acceptance: π_*(U) ⊗ ℚ is ℚ in odd degrees (SSAT Example 1.25).
RP^{2n} shows the abelian hypothesis is needed (SSAT p. 38).
Borel's computation of K_n(O_F) ⊗ ℚ uses H_*(BGL(O_F)⁺; ℚ) = stable cohomology of arithmetic groups (BorelRegulators:R.3).

sources.locator: Chapter 1, Theorem 1.24 and the paragraph after its proof, pp. 38–39
sources.match: Cartan–Serre for abelian spaces and its application to H-spaces.

nodes.title: The core of a symmetric monoidal category is a symmetric monoidal groupoid
nodes.statement: For a symmetric monoidal category (S, □, e), the core Core S (all objects, only isomorphisms) inherits a symmetric monoidal structure: □ restricts to isomorphisms and the unit, associativity and symmetry constraints are isomorphisms. A symmetric monoidal groupoid is a symmetric monoidal category all of whose morphisms are invertible; Core is the right adjoint of the inclusion of symmetric monoidal groupoids into symmetric monoidal categories with strong monoidal functors. Examples: Core of finitely generated projective R-modules under ⊕ (not strict in the sense of Bhatt–Scholze Definition 12.1, i.e. c_{M,M} is the swap, not the identity; this is unrelated to strict associativity), finite sets under ⊔, based free modules F(R) = ⊔_n GL_n(R) under block sum, Pic(R) under ⊗.
hypotheses: S symmetric monoidal (Mathlib MonoidalCategory + SymmetricCategory); direct sum is not assumed strictly associative or strictly commutative.
proofSteps: The tensor product of two isomorphisms is an isomorphism, and the structure isomorphisms of S lie in Core S, so the coherence axioms hold there (Bhatt–Scholze p. 54; Weibel IV Definition 4.1).
Strong monoidal functors S → T restrict to Core.
acceptance: π₀(B Core S) is the commutative monoid of isomorphism classes S^iso.
For projective modules the symmetry c_{M,M} is not the identity when M ≠ 0 (Bhatt–Scholze Example 12.2(i)).

nodes.title: The classifying space of a symmetric monoidal category is a homotopy-commutative H-space
nodes.statement: For a symmetric monoidal category S with countably many morphisms (or with products taken in compactly generated spaces), BS is an H-space with multiplication B(□) ∘ (B(S × S) ≅ BS × BS)⁻¹ and unit the vertex [e]; it is homotopy associative and homotopy commutative, π₀(BS) is the commutative monoid of components and H₀(BS; ℤ) = ℤ[π₀ BS]. If e is initial in S (e.g. S additive), BS is contractible.
hypotheses: The homeomorphism B(S × S) ≅ BS × BS (H.1/classifying-space-prod) needs a finite factor or compactly generated products; for countable CW complexes the ordinary product is already a CW complex, which covers S = F(R) for countable R. In general B(□) is continuous only on the compactly generated product, so Mathlib's HSpace (multiplication on the ordinary product X × X) applies only when BS × BS already has the CW topology; the general case needs a compactly generated variant of H-spaces (packet gap 'Realisation of products').
proofSteps: The unit isomorphisms e □ s ≅ s ≅ s □ e are natural transformations, hence homotopies (H.1/natural-transformations-adjoints-contractibility), making [e] a two-sided unit up to homotopy rel [e] after the standard modification; associativity and symmetry constraints give the homotopies (Weibel IV §4 opening).
If e is initial, BS is contractible (H.1/contractible-of-initial-or-terminal).

Modify B(□) within its homotopy class so that it is strictly unital at the vertex [e] and the two unit homotopies are relative to [e], as Mathlib's HSpace requires: use the edges of λ_e, ρ_e and the homotopy extension property of the CW pair (BS × BS, BS ∨ BS) (tauceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4).
acceptance: B(Finset under ⊔) is contractible but B(Core) ≃ ⊔ BΣ_n is not (Weibel IV §4 opening and 4.1.1(a)).
For S = Pic(R), B Pic(R) ≃ Pic(R) × B(R^×) (Weibel IV Example 4.1.1(d)).

sources.match: Weibel's statement and its derivation from 3.1(6).

nodes.title: Quillen's S⁻¹S construction for a symmetric monoidal groupoid
nodes.statement: For a symmetric monoidal groupoid S in which translations Aut(s) → Aut(s □ t) are injective, S⁻¹S has objects pairs (m, n) and morphisms equivalence classes of composites (m₁, m₂) → (s □ m₁, s □ m₂) → (n₁, n₂), two composites being equivalent when an isomorphism α : s ≅ t identifies their second parts. S⁻¹S is symmetric monoidal with (m, n) □ (m′, n′) = (m □ m′, n □ n′), m ↦ (m, e) is monoidal, and K(S) := B(S⁻¹S), K_n(S) := π_n B(S⁻¹S). A strict monoidal functor S → T induces S⁻¹S → T⁻¹T.
hypotheses: Every morphism of S an isomorphism; translations faithful (not needed to define S⁻¹S; it makes each morphism determine s, f, g up to unique isomorphism, which Exercise 4.5 and Theorem 4.8 use).
proofSteps: Define S⁻¹S as ⟨S, S × S⟩ for the diagonal action (H.4/monoidal-action-category), equivalently by Weibel's explicit description (Definition 4.2, Explanation 4.2.1).
The monoidal structure is componentwise (Remark 4.2.2); there is a morphism (e, e) → (m, n) □ (n, m) giving inverses on π₀, not natural (Exercise 4.3).
acceptance: Pic(R) with π₀ already a group gives K₀ = Pic(R), K₁ = R^× and K_n = 0 for n ≥ 2 (Weibel IV Example 4.4.2).
There is no natural transformation 0 ⇒ id □ ι on S⁻¹S (Weibel IV Exercise 4.3): the homotopy inverse is not given by a natural transformation.
Do not use the nerve of all projective-module maps; BP(R) is contractible, only iso P(R) carries the group completion input.

sources.locator: Definition 4.2, Explanation 4.2.1, Remark 4.2.2, Definition 4.3, pp. IV.37–38

nodes.title: Actions of monoidal categories and the categories ⟨S, X⟩ and S⁻¹X
nodes.statement: A monoidal category S acts on a category X by a functor □ : S × X → X with coherent natural isomorphisms s □ (t □ x) ≅ (s □ t) □ x and e □ x ≅ x. The category ⟨S, X⟩ has the objects of X and morphisms x → y equivalence classes of pairs (s, φ : s □ x → y), (s, φ) ∼ (s′, φ′) when an isomorphism s ≅ s′ identifies φ′ with φ. Write S⁻¹X = ⟨S, S × X⟩ for the diagonal action; S⁻¹S is the case X = S. If S is symmetric, S acts on S⁻¹X by s □ (t, x) = (s □ t, x), and this action is invertible (each translation a homotopy equivalence).
hypotheses: S monoidal (symmetric for the action on S⁻¹X); X any category; for S a groupoid with faithful translations, morphisms of ⟨S, X⟩ have unique representatives up to unique isomorphism.
proofSteps: Define ⟨S, X⟩ by Weibel's Definition 4.7.1, as the translation category of the action (compare H.1/translation-category-classifying-space for monoids acting on sets).

Invertibility of the action on S⁻¹X: the natural transformation (t, x) ↦ (s □ t, s □ x) relates the translation by s with the other-coordinate translation, giving a homotopy inverse (Weibel IV Definition 4.7.1).
acceptance: If every arrow of S is an isomorphism, e is initial in ⟨S, S⟩ and B⟨S, S⟩ is contractible.
For S = ℕ acting on ⊔ X_n via a sequence X₀ → X₁ → ⋯, ⟨ℕ, X⟩ is the mapping telescope (Weibel IV Exercise 4.2).

sources.match: Weibel's definitions of actions, ⟨S, X⟩ and S⁻¹X, with the invertibility remark.

S⁻¹S → S⁻¹X → ⟨S, X⟩ is a homotopy fibration for monic X
the + = Q theorem uses ⟨S, EA⟩ and S⁻¹EA (Weibel IV §7)

nodes.title: π₀ of S⁻¹S is the Grothendieck group of the monoid of components
nodes.statement: The canonical map from the Grothendieck group of the commutative monoid π₀(S) = S^iso to π₀ B(S⁻¹S) induced by m ↦ (m, e) is an isomorphism of abelian groups, inverse to (m, n) ↦ [m] − [n]. Hence K₀(S) = π₀ B(S⁻¹S) agrees with Mathlib's Algebra.GrothendieckGroup of the monoid of isomorphism classes, and for S = Core of an essentially small additive category with ⊞ with Tau Ceti's SplitK0.
hypotheses: S symmetric monoidal groupoid with faithful translations.
proofSteps: The function α(m, n) = [m] − [n] is invariant along both kinds of morphisms of S⁻¹S, hence defines π₀ B(S⁻¹S) → Algebra.GrothendieckGroup π₀(S) (H.1/pi0-classifying-space); it is inverse to the map from the universal property (Algebra.GrothendieckGroup.lift) (Weibel IV Lemma 4.3.1).
Compare with TauCeti.SplitK0.grothendieckAddGroupEquiv for additive categories, through TauCeti.ObjectCode A = Shrink (Skeleton A) and Multiplicative.
acceptance: For S = F(R) (based free modules), K₀(S) = ℤ, not K₀(R).
For S = iso P(R), K₀(S) = K₀(R).

sources.match: Weibel's Lemma 4.3.1 and its proof.

nodes.title: Group completions of homotopy-commutative H-spaces
nodes.statement: For an H-space X whose multiplication is associative and commutative up to homotopy, an H-map f : X → Y to another H-space Y is a group completion when π₀(Y) is the group completion of the commutative monoid π₀(X) (via f) and, for every commutative ring k, the induced map identifies H_*(Y; k) with the localisation π₀(X)⁻¹ H_*(X; k) of the Pontryagin ring at the multiplicative set π₀(X) ⊂ H₀(X; k). When X is a CW complex, Y is taken to be one, and is then group-like.
hypotheses: X, Y H-spaces (Mathlib HSpace, so the multiplication is continuous on the ordinary product; see H.4/classifying-space-hspace for when BS qualifies) that are homotopy associative and commutative; Y a CW complex when X is.
proofSteps: Define IsGroupCompletion f by the π₀ condition (Algebra.GrothendieckGroup universal map is an isomorphism) and the homology condition for all k (Weibel IV Definition 4.4).
The Pontryagin product makes H_*(X; k) a graded-commutative ring with H₀ = k[π₀X] (Weibel IV p. 38, citing [Wh, III.7]).
acceptance: For a group-like X, the identity is a group completion (Weibel IV Lemma 4.4.1).
BS → B(S⁻¹S) is a group completion (H.4/quillen-localization-of-homology).

sources.match: Weibel's Definition 4.4, including the homology localisation condition for all commutative rings k.

uses.how: B(S⁻¹S) is a group completion of BS
Z × BGL(R)⁺ is a group completion of ⊔ BGL_n(R)
GW^s_cl(ℤ) is defined as the homotopy-theoretic group completion of the groupoid of forms

nodes.title: The projection S⁻¹X → ⟨S, S⟩ is cofibred
nodes.statement: If S = Core S has faithful translations and S acts on X, the projection ρ : S⁻¹X → ⟨S, S⟩, (s, x) ↦ s, is cofibred (precofibred with cobase changes composing coherently) with fibre over s isomorphic to X, the cobase change along a morphism of ⟨S, S⟩ represented by (t, t □ s ≅ s′) being the translation x ↦ t □ x.
hypotheses: S a symmetric monoidal groupoid with faithful translations.
proofSteps: Construct, for each (s, x) and each morphism s → s′ of ⟨S, S⟩, a cocartesian lift using the representative (t, φ); faithfulness of translations makes the representative unique up to unique isomorphism, so the lift is well defined (Weibel IV Exercise 4.5, Quillen; statement only in the source, proof packet-authored).
acceptance: For X = point, ρ is the identity of ⟨S, S⟩.
Used with H.2/functor-homology-spectral-sequence in the proof of Theorem 4.8.

sources.match: Weibel's exercise (attributed to Quillen).

nodes.title: Invertible actions do not change the homotopy type
nodes.statement: If S = Core S has faithful translations and acts invertibly on X (each translation X → X a homotopy equivalence), then each functor X → S⁻¹X, x ↦ (s, x), is a homotopy equivalence. In particular S⁻¹Y ≃ S⁻¹(S⁻¹Y) for every category Y with an S-action.
hypotheses: S a symmetric monoidal groupoid with faithful translations; the action on X invertible.
proofSteps: ρ : S⁻¹X → ⟨S, S⟩ is cofibred with fibre X and cobase changes the translations, which are homotopy equivalences (H.4/action-projection-cofibred); Theorem B for cofibred functors (H.2/quillen-theorem-b-prefibred) gives a homotopy fibre sequence X → S⁻¹X → ⟨S, S⟩, and ⟨S, S⟩ is contractible (Weibel IV Exercise 4.6 hint); so x ↦ (s, x) is a weak equivalence of CW complexes, hence a homotopy equivalence (Whitehead).
acceptance: S acts invertibly on S⁻¹Y, giving S⁻¹Y ≃ S⁻¹(S⁻¹Y).
For X = S with the regular action, which is not invertible unless π₀(S) is a group, the conclusion fails: S → S⁻¹S is not a homotopy equivalence for S = F(R).

sources.match: Weibel's exercise with its hint.

nodes.title: Quillen's theorem: S⁻¹X localises homology; B(S⁻¹S) is a group completion
nodes.statement: Let S be a symmetric monoidal groupoid with faithful translations acting on a category X, and S⁻¹X = ⟨S, S × X⟩. Then the map (π₀S)⁻¹H_q(X; k) → H_q(S⁻¹X; k) induced by x ↦ (e, x) is an isomorphism for all q and every commutative ring k. In particular BS → B(S⁻¹S) is a group completion (H.4/group-completion).
hypotheses: Every map in S is an isomorphism; translations Aut(s) → Aut(s □ t) are injective.
proofSteps: The projection ρ : S⁻¹X → ⟨S, S⟩ is cofibred with fibre X (H.4/action-projection-cofibred).
The homology spectral sequence of the cofibred functor ρ has E²_{pq} = H_p(⟨S, S⟩; H_q(X)) ⇒ H_{p+q}(S⁻¹X) (H.2/functor-homology-spectral-sequence).

S acts on ρ over the identity of ⟨S, S⟩ by (t, x) ↦ (t, s □ x) (a map of cofibred functors, using the symmetry of S); by naturality of H.2/functor-homology-spectral-sequence the spectral sequence is one of ℤ[π₀S]-modules, acting on E² through the translations of H_q(X) and on the abutment through translations of S⁻¹X, which are homotopy equivalences (H.4/monoidal-action-category).
Localising at π₀S ⊂ H₀(S) is exact and π₀S already acts invertibly on H_*(S⁻¹X), giving E²_{pq} = H_p(⟨S, S⟩; M_q) with M_q = (π₀S)⁻¹H_q(X).

Each M_q is morphism-inverting, hence a local system on B⟨S, S⟩ (H.1/local-systems-as-functors), and ⟨S, S⟩ is contractible because e is initial; so H_p(⟨S, S⟩; M_q) vanishes for p ≠ 0 (H.1/homology-of-small-categories) and the spectral sequence degenerates (Weibel IV Theorem 4.8 proof, following Grayson's 'Higher algebraic K-theory II', p. 221, not read).
The group completion statement follows with Remark 4.2.2 and H.4/S-inverse-S-pi0.
acceptance: K₁(S) = colim_s H₁(Aut(s); ℤ) (Weibel IV Corollary 4.8.1).
Barratt–Priddy–Quillen–Segal: for finite sets K(Sets_fin) ≃ ℤ × BΣ_∞⁺ (Weibel IV 4.9.2–4.9.3; the identification with Ω^∞S^∞ is cited, not proved).

sources.locator: Definitions 4.7, 4.7.1, (4.7.2) and Theorem 4.8 with proof, pp. IV.41–42
sources.match: Theorem 4.8; the proof steps follow Weibel's proof and the two exercises it invokes.

nodes.title: Group completions of group-like H-spaces
nodes.statement: If X is a group-like H-space (CW), X is its own group completion and every group completion f : X → Y is a homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: X, Y homotopy-associative, homotopy-commutative H-spaces of CW type; X group-like (π₀ X a group, equivalently a homotopy inverse exists for CW X).
proofSteps: f is a homology isomorphism with all coefficients k, hence an isomorphism on π₀ and on π₁ = H₁ of the (abelian) basepoint components.

On basepoint components f is a plus construction relative to the trivial subgroup into an H-space; by H.3/plus-hspace-recognition (abelian targets) or directly H.3/hspace-homology-whitehead it is a homotopy equivalence (Weibel IV Lemma 4.4.1, which invokes Theorem 1.5).

For a component X_c, f|X_c is homotopic to L_{f(x)} ∘ f|X₀ ∘ L_{x⁻¹} for x ∈ X_c, and left translations by points are homotopy equivalences between components by homotopy associativity, so f is a homotopy equivalence on every component.
acceptance: Pic(R): S and S⁻¹S are homotopy equivalent (Weibel IV Example 4.4.2).
ℤ × BGL(R)⁺ is a group completion of ⊔ BGL_n(R) directly (Weibel IV Exercise 4.9).

sources.match: Weibel's Lemma 4.4.1.

nodes.title: Uniqueness of group completions up to phantom maps
nodes.statement: Group completions are not unique up to homotopy when phantom maps exist: if f : X → Y is a group completion and φ is phantom, f + φ is a weak H-map satisfying the π₀ and homology conditions of H.4/group-completion, and is not homotopic to f in general. If π₀(X) is countable or has a countable cofinal submonoid, any two group completions f′ : X → X′, f″ : X → X″ are related by a homotopy equivalence g : X′ → X″, unique up to weak homotopy, with g ∘ f′ weakly homotopic to f″.
hypotheses: H-spaces of CW type; countability of π₀(X) or of a cofinal submonoid.
proofSteps: Phantom perturbations preserve the defining homology and π₀ conditions (Weibel IV p. 39).
The uniqueness theorem is Caradus–Clarke–McGibbon–Thomason [CCMT, 1.2], quoted by Weibel; its proof is not read (packet gap 'CCMT uniqueness of group completions').
acceptance: Exhibit the dependence of uniqueness on countability; do not state strict uniqueness up to homotopy in general.

sources.locator: Phantom maps paragraph and Theorem 4.4.3, p. IV.39
sources.match: Introduces Theorem 4.4.3 as quoted from [CCMT, 1.2].

nodes.title: The fibration S⁻¹S → S⁻¹X → ⟨S, X⟩
nodes.statement: Suppose every map of X is monic and each translation Aut_S(s) → Aut_X(s □ x) is injective. Then for each object x of X the sequence S⁻¹S → S⁻¹X → ⟨S, X⟩ (s ↦ s □ x, then projection to the second factor) is a homotopy fibre sequence. In particular, if ⟨S, X⟩ is contractible then S⁻¹S → S⁻¹X is a homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: Every morphism of X monic; translations into Aut_X(s □ x) injective; S a symmetric monoidal groupoid with faithful translations.
proofSteps: π : S⁻¹X → ⟨S, X⟩ and S⁻¹π : S⁻¹(S⁻¹X) → ⟨S, X⟩ are precofibred with fibres S and S⁻¹S over x and cobase changes the translations; this uses that every map of X is monic and that the translations Aut_S(s) → Aut_X(s □ x) are injective, which give unique representatives (H.2/prefibred-iff-fibre-adjoint; Weibel IV Exercise 4.7 hint).

The cobase changes of S⁻¹π are homotopy equivalences because S acts invertibly on S⁻¹S (H.4/monoidal-action-category), so H.2/quillen-theorem-b-prefibred gives the homotopy fibre sequence S⁻¹S → S⁻¹(S⁻¹X) → ⟨S, X⟩.
S⁻¹X ≃ S⁻¹(S⁻¹X) by H.4/invertible-action-equivalence, and the composite S⁻¹S → S⁻¹X is (m, n) ↦ (m, n □ x).
acceptance: Used in the + = Q theorem: ⟨S, EA⟩ contractible gives S⁻¹S ≃ S⁻¹EA (GeneralAlgebraicKTheory:K.2:plus, Weibel IV §7).
The invertibility statement 4.7.1 is the special case of the action of S on S⁻¹X.

sources.match: Weibel's exercise and hint; the proof outline is packet-authored from the hint.

nodes.title: A product of plus constructions is a plus construction
nodes.statement: Let f : X → X′ be a plus construction relative to P ⊆ π₁X and g : Y → Y′ one relative to Q ⊆ π₁Y (connected CW complexes). Then f × g : X × Y → X′ × Y′ is a plus construction relative to P × Q ⊆ π₁X × π₁Y = π₁(X × Y). In particular (BG × BH)⁺ ≃ BG⁺ × BH⁺ under BG × BH, and BGL(R₁ × R₂)⁺ ≃ BGL(R₁)⁺ × BGL(R₂)⁺.
hypotheses: Connected CW complexes; products in compactly generated spaces or with one factor countable (packet gap 'Realisation of products'); P, Q perfect normal.
proofSteps: The homotopy fibre of f × g over (x′, y′) is the product of the homotopy fibres (H.2/homotopy-fibre-and-long-exact-sequence).
A product of acyclic spaces is acyclic by the Künneth theorem (tauceti AlgebraicTopology stage 5); so f × g is acyclic (H.3/acyclic-map).
π₁ of a product is the product of the π₁, so ker π₁(f × g) = P × Q (H.3/plus-construction-predicate).
acceptance: Used for the H-space structure on BGL(R)⁺ (H.4/plus-hspace-block-sum) and the H-map property of H.4/gl-plus-comparison-naturality.

sources.match: Weibel's exercise for the product of two rings; its content is that a product of plus constructions is a plus construction. The general lemma is packet-authored (it belongs with H.3's plus construction and may be moved there).

nodes.title: Block sum makes BGL(R)⁺ an H-space and ℤ × BGL(R)⁺ a group completion
nodes.statement: For a ring R, the block-sum homomorphisms GL_m(R) × GL_n(R) → GL_{m+n}(R) ⊂ GL(R) induce maps BGL_m(R) × BGL_n(R) → BGL(R)⁺ which assemble, via the universal property of the plus construction, into a homotopy-associative, homotopy-commutative H-space structure on BGL(R)⁺, natural in R up to homotopy; the resulting map ⊔_n BGL_n(R) → ℤ × BGL(R)⁺ is an H-space map and a group completion (H.4/group-completion), with π₁ = K₁(R) acting trivially on all π_n.
hypotheses: R a ring; plus construction relative to E(R), which is perfect and normal (KTheoryLowDegrees:U.1).
proofSteps: The interleaving homomorphism ⊕ : GL(R) × GL(R) → GL(R) (first factor on odd, second on even coordinates), whose restriction to GL_m × GL_n is conjugate by a permutation matrix to block sum GL_m × GL_n → GL_{m+n} (so the induced maps are freely homotopic, H.1/conjugate-homomorphisms-freely-homotopic), induces BGL(R) × BGL(R) → BGL(R) → BGL(R)⁺, which kills E(R) × E(R) on π₁, and (BGL(R) × BGL(R))⁺ ≃ BGL(R)⁺ × BGL(R)⁺ (Weibel IV Exercise 1.7), so it factors through BGL(R)⁺ × BGL(R)⁺ (this uses the universal property of H.3/plus-construction-universal-property for the target BGL(R)⁺, which is not yet known to be abelian: the packet gap 'Plus-construction universal property for non-abelian targets'; Weibel IV Exercise 1.11).

Homotopy associativity and commutativity: conjugation by permutation matrices relates the two orders and induces maps homotopic to the identity on BGL(R)⁺ (inner automorphisms act trivially, H.1/conjugate-homomorphisms-freely-homotopic, after plus).
The group-completion property: H_*(ℤ × BGL(R)⁺) = ℤ[t, t⁻¹] ⊗ colim H_*(BGL_n(R)) = (π₀)⁻¹H_*(⊔ BGL_n(R)) (Weibel IV Exercise 4.9).
acceptance: The H-space BGL(R)⁺ is abelian, so π₁ = K₁(R) acts trivially on K_n(R) (H.3/hspace-is-abelian), as BorelRegulators requires.
BGL(ℤ)⁺ has π₁ = ℤ/2.

sources.locator: Exercise 1.11, p. IV.15; Exercise 4.9, p. IV.46
sources.match: Weibel's exercises establishing the block-sum H-space structure and the direct group-completion statement.

nodes.title: The symmetric monoidal groupoid F(R) of based free modules and its functor to iso P(R)
nodes.statement: For a ring R, F(R) is the groupoid with objects n ∈ ℕ (the based free module Rⁿ), Hom(n, n) = GL_n(R) (Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup (Fin n) R) and no maps between m ≠ n, composition g ≫ h := g * h. It is a strict symmetric monoidal groupoid: m □ n = m + n, g □ h = block sum (Matrix.fromBlocks g 0 0 h reindexed along finSumFinEquiv), unit 0, identity associators and unitors, symmetry c_{m,n} the permutation matrix exchanging the two blocks. With Mathlib's left modules and the KTheoryLowDegrees Z.1 convention (matrices act on row vectors from the right), n ↦ Rⁿ = (Fin n → R), g ↦ vecMulLinear g is a strong symmetric monoidal functor F(R) ⥤ iso P(R) (the core of finitely generated projective left R-modules under ⊕); it is bijective on the automorphism group of each object for every ring R, injective on isomorphism classes iff R has the invariant basis property, and cofinal.
hypotheses: R an associative unital ring; the zero ring is allowed (then all Rⁿ are 0 in iso P(R) but distinct in F(R)).

iso P(R) is the core of the full subcategory of ModuleCat R on finitely generated projective modules, symmetric monoidal by the biproduct (Mathlib's monoidal structure from finite (co)products), as in KTheoryLowDegrees:Z.1.
proofSteps: Define the groupoid and the strict symmetric monoidal structure from block sums; associativity and unit are equalities of matrices after reindexing (Matrix.fromBlocks, finSumFinEquiv), the hexagon and symmetry identities are identities of permutation matrices.

With row vectors, vecMulLinear (g * h) = vecMulLinear h ∘ vecMulLinear g, so g ↦ vecMulLinear g is covariant for g ≫ h := g * h; the monoidal structure isomorphisms R^m ⊕ Rⁿ ≅ R^{m+n} are the coordinate splittings (KTheoryLowDegrees:Z.1/idempotent-module-block).
Faithful translations: g ↦ g □ 1 is injective. Cofinality in iso P(R): every finitely generated projective P has P ⊕ Q ≅ Rⁿ (KTheoryLowDegrees:Z.1/free-summand-data).
acceptance: Isomorphism classes of F(R) are ℕ, so K₀(F(R)) = ℤ (H.4/S-inverse-S-pi0), whereas K₀(iso P(R)) = K₀(R).

nodes.title: B(S⁻¹S) ≃ ℤ × BGL(R)⁺ for based free modules
nodes.statement: For a ring R let S = F(R) = ⊔_n GL_n(R), the symmetric monoidal groupoid of based free modules Rⁿ under concatenation and block sum. Then B(S⁻¹S) is a group completion of BS and B(S⁻¹S) ≃ ℤ × BGL(R)⁺, the basepoint component Y_S receiving an acyclic map from BGL(R) (via the mapping telescope) that is a plus construction relative to E(R). The product decomposition is a space-level statement after choosing component representatives; it is not a natural splitting of infinite loop spaces.
hypotheses: E(R) = [GL(R), GL(R)] is a perfect normal subgroup of GL(R) (Whitehead; KTheoryLowDegrees:U.1).
The product decomposition uses translations between components, which are not natural (Weibel IV 1.1.2).
proofSteps: The homomorphisms η_n : GL_n(R) → Aut_{S⁻¹S}(Rⁿ, Rⁿ), g ↦ (g, 1), are compatible with stabilisation up to the natural transformation η ⇒ η(□R), giving a map from the mapping telescope of BGL_n(R) into the basepoint component Y_S (Weibel IV proof of Theorem 4.9; the telescope category ∫_ℕ GL_•(R) = ⟨ℕ, ⊔ GL_n(R)⟩ maps to the one-object category GL(R) with contractible comma categories, so its classifying space is BGL(R) up to homotopy, H.2/quillen-theorem-a).

By Theorem 4.8, H_*(B(S⁻¹S)) is the localisation of H_*(BS) at {eⁿ}, i.e. the colimit along ⊕R, so H_*(B(S⁻¹S)) ≅ H_*(Y_S) ⊗ ℤ[e, e⁻¹] with H_*(Y_S) ≅ colim H_*(BGL_n(R)) = H_*(BGL(R)) (H.1/filtered-colimit-homology).

Thus BGL(R) → Y_S is an integral homology isomorphism into an H-space, so H.3/plus-hspace-recognition gives BGL(R)⁺ ≃ Y_S and the map is acyclic (BGL(R)⁺ is an H-space by H.4/plus-hspace-block-sum, as H.3/plus-hspace-recognition requires). Finally B(S⁻¹S) ≃ ℤ × Y_S because π₀ = ℤ is a group and translation by a vertex of component n is a homotopy equivalence Y_S → Y_n (homotopy associativity); this choice of translations is not natural.
acceptance: The components of B(S⁻¹S) are indexed by ℤ = K₀(F(R)), not by K₀(R).
Ring-map naturality and the H-map property for block sum are H.4/gl-plus-comparison-naturality; translations between components are not natural.

sources.match: Displayed conclusion of Theorem 4.9, proved by the telescope and homology-localisation argument recorded above.

nodes.title: The telescope map into the group completion is acyclic
nodes.statement: Let S be a symmetric monoidal groupoid with faithful translations and a cofinal sequence s_{n+1} = s_n □ a_n, Aut(S) = colim_n Aut(s_n). Then the map B Aut(S) → Y_S from the mapping telescope into the basepoint component of B(S⁻¹S) is acyclic: its homotopy fibre is acyclic, equivalently it induces isomorphisms on homology with every local coefficient system pulled back from Y_S. An integral homology isomorphism into an H-space is not enough for this in general.
hypotheses: S a symmetric monoidal groupoid with faithful translations and a sequence of objects s_{n+1} = s_n □ a_n that is cofinal (every s has s′ with s □ s′ ≅ s_n for some n); Aut(S) = colim_n Aut(s_n). The map B Aut(S) → Y_S is defined here: the homomorphisms Aut(s_n) → Aut_{S⁻¹S}(s_n, s_n), g ↦ (g, 1), are compatible with stabilisation by a_n up to a natural transformation, which gives a functor from the telescope category ⟨ℕ, ⊔_n Aut(s_n)⟩ to S⁻¹S. Its classifying space is B Aut(S) up to homotopy (H.2/quillen-theorem-a).
proofSteps: The map is an integral homology isomorphism by H.4/quillen-localization-of-homology (as in Weibel IV Theorem 4.9).

Acyclicity: the local-coefficient group-completion theorem (McDuff–Segal 1976; Randal-Williams 2013, Corollary 1.2), cited by Calmès et al. for exactly this step; not read: packet gap 'Local-coefficient group completion theorem'. For S = F(R) it also follows from H.3/plus-hspace-recognition, since BGL(R)⁺ is an H-space (H.4/plus-hspace-block-sum).
acceptance: Counterexample to the constant-coefficient shortcut: a CW complex Z with π₁Z = ℤ, π₂Z = ℤ[t^±]/(2t − 1) and H̃_*(Z) = H̃_*(S¹) maps to S¹ by an integral homology isomorphism that is not acyclic.
For finite sets it gives the acyclic map BΣ_∞ → Ω₀B N(Fin_*).

sources.match: Calmès et al. cite McDuff–Segal and Randal-Williams for the identification of the positive component with the plus construction.
Weibel asserts the acyclicity without proof.

uses.how: the telescope map is a plus construction

nodes.title: Group completion with a cofinal sequence of objects
nodes.statement: Let S = Core S be a symmetric monoidal groupoid with faithful translations and a cofinal sequence s_{n+1} = s_n □ a_n (every s has s′ with s □ s′ ≅ s_n for some n), and Aut(S) = colim_n Aut(s_n). Then the commutator subgroup E of Aut(S) is perfect and normal, K₁(S) = Aut(S)/E, the plus construction B Aut(S)⁺ relative to E is the basepoint component of B(S⁻¹S), and B(S⁻¹S) ≃ K₀(S) × B Aut(S)⁺.
hypotheses: S has a cofinal sequence as stated; faithful translations.
E = [Aut(S), Aut(S)] (automatically normal); its perfectness is part of the conclusion.
proofSteps: The mapping telescope gives a map B Aut(S) → Y_S that is an integral homology isomorphism (H.4/quillen-localization-of-homology, as in Theorem 4.9) and is acyclic by H.4/group-completion-acyclic (McDuff–Segal, Randal-Williams 2013, recorded gap); an acyclic map with kernel E on π₁ is a plus construction (H.3/plus-construction-predicate) (Weibel IV Theorem 4.10 proof).

By H.4/group-completion-acyclic and H.3/acyclic-map, π₁(B Aut(S)) = Aut(S) → π₁(Y_S) is onto with perfect kernel P. P ⊆ E since P = [P, P]. E ⊆ P since π₁(Y_S) is abelian, as Y_S is a component of the H-space B(S⁻¹S) (H.4/classifying-space-hspace, H.3/hspace-is-abelian). Hence E = P is perfect, K₁(S) = π₁(Y_S) = Aut(S)/E, and the telescope map is a plus construction relative to E. (Weibel instead cites Bass p. 355 for the perfectness of E; that route is not needed.)
acceptance: Finite sets: B(S⁻¹S) ≃ ℤ × BΣ_∞⁺ (Barratt–Priddy–Quillen–Segal, Weibel IV 4.9.3).
Free G-sets: K(G-Sets_fin) ≃ ℤ × B(G ≀ Σ_∞)⁺ (Weibel IV Example 4.10.1).

Hermitian forms over ℤ: the positive components of the classical Grothendieck–Witt spaces are plus constructions of the infinite orthogonal and symplectic groups (H.4/hermitian-group-completion-integers).

ε-quadratic forms over a number ring O: every form is an orthogonal summand of an ε-hyperbolic form, so with the hyperbolic sequence every component of the quadratic Grothendieck–Witt space is B O_{∞,∞}(O)⁺ for ε = 1 and B Sp^q_∞(O)⁺ for ε = −1 (Calmès et al. Remark 2.3.20).
Quadratic forms: K(Quad^ε(A)) ≃ εL₀(A) × BεO⁺ (Weibel IV Example 4.12.2).

sources.match: Weibel's Theorem 4.10 and its proof citing Bass p. 355.
The hyperbolic forms form the cofinal sequence of this theorem; the remark's conclusion is its plus-construction identification.

nodes.title: Cofinality for actions: S⁻¹X ≃ T⁻¹X
nodes.statement: Let f : S → T be a cofinal strong monoidal functor of symmetric monoidal groupoids with faithful translations, and let T act on a category X. Then S acts on X through f, S acts invertibly on X iff T does, and B(S⁻¹X) ≃ B(T⁻¹X) through S⁻¹X → T⁻¹(S⁻¹X) ≅ S⁻¹(T⁻¹X) ← T⁻¹X.
hypotheses: f cofinal: for every t there are t′ and s with t □ t′ ≅ f(s).
proofSteps: If t □ t′ ≅ f(s), the translation by t has a right homotopy inverse up to the equivalence f(s) □ − and, using the symmetry, a left one; natural isomorphisms give homotopies (H.1/natural-transformations-adjoints-contractibility); so invertibility for S and for T are equivalent.
T⁻¹(S⁻¹X) and S⁻¹(T⁻¹X) are both isomorphic to ⟨S × T, S × T × X⟩ (direct check from Definition 4.7.1).
S and T act invertibly on S⁻¹X and T⁻¹X (H.4/monoidal-action-category), so H.4/invertible-action-equivalence gives the two outer homotopy equivalences (Weibel IV proof of Theorem 4.11(a)).
acceptance: For X = T this gives B(S⁻¹T) ≃ B(T⁻¹T).

sources.locator: Cofinality Theorem 4.11(a) with proof, p. IV.44
sources.match: Part (a) of Weibel's Theorem 4.11, split from H.4/cofinality-theorem.

nodes.title: Quillen's cofinality theorem for symmetric monoidal groupoids
nodes.statement: Let f : S → T be a cofinal strong monoidal functor of symmetric monoidal groupoids with faithful translations (for every t there are t′ and s with t □ t′ ≅ f(s)) inducing isomorphisms Aut_S(s) ≅ Aut_T(f s). Then the map Y_S → Y_T of basepoint components induced by f⁻¹f : S⁻¹S → T⁻¹T is a homotopy equivalence, so K_n(S) ≅ K_n(T) for n ≥ 1 (K₀ may differ).
hypotheses: f cofinal and strong monoidal (strict monoidality is not assumed: F(R) → iso P(R) is only strong), inducing isomorphisms on automorphism groups; S and T have faithful translations.
proofSteps: f induces f⁻¹f : S⁻¹S → T⁻¹T (H.4/strictification-independence) and an H-space map Y_S → Y_T.

Theorem 4.8 and B(S) ≃ ⊔ B Aut(s) (H.1/groupoid-nerve-one-type) give H_*(Y_S) = colim_{s∈S} H_*(B Aut(s)) = colim_{s∈S} H_*(B Aut(fs)) ≅ colim_{t∈T} H_*(B Aut(t)) = H_*(Y_T) using cofinality of the translation categories (H.4/quillen-localization-of-homology). The isomorphism (4.7.2) is natural for f: x ↦ (e, x) commutes with f⁻¹f up to the unit isomorphism f(e) ≅ e, and natural isomorphisms give homotopies (H.1/natural-transformations-adjoints-contractibility). So the composite isomorphism is the map induced by Y_S → Y_T.
The induced H-space map Y_S → Y_T is an integral homology isomorphism of connected H-spaces, hence a homotopy equivalence (H.3/hspace-homology-whitehead).
acceptance: The one-object subcategory R^× is cofinal in Pic(R) (Weibel IV p. 44).
F(R) → iso P(R) is cofinal (H.4/cofinality-projective-modules).

sources.locator: Cofinality Theorem 4.11 with proof, pp. IV.44–45

nodes.title: Cofinality: the group completion of iso P(R) is K₀(R) × BGL(R)⁺
nodes.statement: For a ring R and S = iso P(R) (finitely generated projective modules and isomorphisms, under ⊕), B(S⁻¹S) ≃ K₀(R) × BGL(R)⁺, the basepoint component being BGL(R)⁺ via the cofinal functor F(R) → iso P(R) (every finitely generated projective module is a direct summand of a finite free module). The identification π₀ B(S⁻¹S) ≅ K₀(R) is the canonical one; the basepoint-component equivalence Y_{iso P(R)} ≃ BGL(R)⁺ is the composite of H.4/gl-telescope-plus-comparison with the cofinality equivalence Y_{F(R)} ≃ Y_{iso P(R)}; its naturality in ring maps up to homotopy is H.4/gl-plus-comparison-naturality. The product decomposition depends on choices of translations and is not natural.
hypotheses: Every finitely generated projective R-module is a direct summand of a finite free module (KTheoryLowDegrees:Z.1).
proofSteps: F(R) → iso P(R) is cofinal (KTheoryLowDegrees:Z.1; Weibel IV Example 4.1.1(c)).
The functor F(R) → iso P(R) of H.4/based-free-module-groupoid is strong symmetric monoidal and bijective on automorphism groups of each Rⁿ (for every ring; injective on objects only under IBN).
Combine H.4/cofinality-theorem with H.4/gl-telescope-plus-comparison for the basepoint component, and H.4/S-inverse-S-pi0 for π₀ = K₀(R) (Weibel IV Corollary 4.11.1).
acceptance: For R = ℤ × ℤ, π₀B(F(R)⁻¹F(R)) = ℤ while π₀B(S⁻¹S) = K₀(R) = ℤ² for S = iso P(R), and the basepoint components agree (both BGL(R)⁺).
Consumers must use this component-preserving comparison, not a claimed natural product splitting.

sources.locator: Corollary 4.11.1, p. IV.45; Example 4.1.1(c), p. IV.36

nodes.title: Naturality of the comparison B(S⁻¹S) ≃ K₀ × BGL(R)⁺
nodes.statement: Let φ : R → R′ be a ring homomorphism and ι_R : BGL(R)⁺ ≃ Y_{F(R)} the equivalence of H.4/gl-telescope-plus-comparison. (i) ι_{R′} ∘ φ⁺ ≃ Y(F(φ)) ∘ ι_R, where φ⁺ is the map of H.3/plus-construction-functoriality and Y(F(φ)) the restriction of B(F(φ)⁻¹F(φ)) to basepoint components. (ii) ι_R is an H-map from the block-sum H-space BGL(R)⁺ (H.4/plus-hspace-block-sum) to Y_{F(R)} with the multiplication induced by ⊕. (iii) The basepoint-component equivalence BGL(R)⁺ ≃ Y_{iso P(R)} of H.4/cofinality-projective-modules is natural in R up to homotopy for base change P ↦ R′ ⊗_R P, and π₀ B(S⁻¹S) ≅ K₀(R) is natural. The decompositions B(S⁻¹S) ≃ K₀ × Y use translations between components and are not natural.
hypotheses: R, R′ rings; all statements up to homotopy.
proofSteps: (i) The telescope maps η_n are strictly natural in R; ι_{R′} ∘ φ⁺ and Y(F(φ)) ∘ ι_R both factor BGL(R) → Y_{F(R′)} through BGL(R)⁺, so they are homotopic by uniqueness in H.3/plus-construction-universal-property (target an H-space, hence abelian by H.3/hspace-is-abelian).

(ii) μ ∘ (ι_R × ι_R) and ι_R ∘ μ⁺ agree up to homotopy after restriction along BGL(R) × BGL(R) → BGL(R)⁺ × BGL(R)⁺, a plus construction by H.4/plus-of-product: both restrict to the map induced by block sum, up to the permutation conjugations of H.1/conjugate-homomorphisms-freely-homotopic; conclude by uniqueness in the universal property with abelian target Y_{F(R)}.

(iii) Base change is strong symmetric monoidal iso P(R) → iso P(R′) and commutes with F(φ) up to monoidal natural isomorphism; apply H.4/strictification-independence and (i); π₀ by H.4/S-inverse-S-pi0.
acceptance: The relative K-theory of Weibel IV 1.11.1 is defined from these maps; K(R) is not naturally the product of K₀(R) and BGL(R)⁺ (Weibel IV 1.1.2).

sources.match: Weibel's statement that the maps are natural only up to homotopy and the splitting is not natural; the H-map and naturality statements are packet-authored from Theorem 4.9 and Exercise 1.11.

nodes.title: Independence of the group completion from strictification
nodes.statement: A strong symmetric monoidal functor F : S → T between symmetric monoidal groupoids with faithful translations induces a functor S⁻¹S → T⁻¹T (well defined up to natural isomorphism, using the monoidal structure isomorphisms of F), and if F is an equivalence of categories then B(S⁻¹S) → B(T⁻¹T) is a homotopy equivalence. Hence K(S) does not depend on replacing S by a strict (or skeletal) model, and naturally isomorphic monoidal functors induce homotopic maps.
hypotheses: F strong symmetric monoidal (structure isomorphisms F(s) □ F(t) ≅ F(s □ t), F(e) ≅ e).
proofSteps: Define F⁻¹F : S⁻¹S → T⁻¹T on objects (m, n) ↦ (Fm, Fn) and on morphisms by transporting (s, f, g) with the structure isomorphisms; coherence (Mathlib's monoidal coherence) makes this a functor.
A monoidal natural isomorphism F ≅ F′ induces a natural isomorphism F⁻¹F ≅ F′⁻¹F′, hence a homotopy (H.1/natural-transformations-adjoints-contractibility).

If F is an equivalence with monoidal inverse G, then G⁻¹G is a homotopy inverse. Alternatively compare homology through H.4/quillen-localization-of-homology. (Weibel IV Exercise 4.4 is the case S^op; the general lemma is packet-authored, answering the roadmap's strictification requirement.)
acceptance: For a field k, F(k) → iso P(k) is a strong symmetric monoidal equivalence from a strictly associative skeleton, so K(F(k)) ≃ K(iso P(k)); likewise Mathlib's Skeleton with its transported monoidal structure gives an equivalent K-theory space.
K(S) ≃ K(S^op) (Weibel IV Exercise 4.4).

sources.match: Weibel's invariance exercise; the general strictification statement is packet-authored.

nodes.title: Special Γ-spaces (E∞-monoids in Segal's model)
nodes.statement: Let Fin_* be the category of finite pointed sets [n] = {0, 1, …, n} pointed at 0. A (special) Γ-space, or E∞-monoid in Segal's strict model, is a functor X : Fin_* ⥤ SSet such that X([0]) is weakly contractible and each Segal map X([n]) → ∏_{i=1}^n X([1]), induced by the maps [n] → [1] collapsing everything except i to 0, is a weak homotopy equivalence (of realisations). For special X, π₀X := π₀|X([1])| is a commutative monoid via [2] → [1] (sending only 0 to 0); X is grouplike if π₀X is a group.
hypotheses: Strict functors to simplicial sets (Kan complexes when needed); the ∞-categorical E∞-monoids of Bhatt–Scholze Definition 12.4 are modelled by these; the strict model is a packet choice, and its comparison with Bhatt–Scholze's ∞-functors (a rectification theorem) is not planned and not used by any H.4 node.
proofSteps: Define the Segal maps and the conditions (Carlsson §1.2 Definition 1; Bhatt–Scholze Definition 12.4).
The monoid structure on π₀ comes from the addition map X([1]) × X([1]) ≃ X([2]) → X([1]) (Bhatt–Scholze p. 56).
acceptance: The constant functor at a point is a special Γ-space with π₀ = 0.
For an abelian group A, [n] ↦ Aⁿ (discrete) is a grouplike special Γ-space.

sources.match: Bhatt–Scholze's definition, of which the strict special Γ-space is the model; π₀ and grouplike from the following paragraphs and Definition 12.7.
Carlsson's Definition 1; his Γ-spaces already satisfy the Segal condition (Π F(p_i) : F(n) → Π F(1) a weak equivalence), i.e. they are the special Γ-spaces of this node.

Bhatt–Scholze §12 builds det : K(R) → Pic^ℤ(R) through E∞-monoids

nodes.title: Segal's Γ-space construction from categories with sums and the delooping machine
nodes.statement: For a category C with a zero object and binary coproducts, Sum_C(X) is the groupoid of summing functors on based subsets of a finite pointed set X: the value at {∗} is a zero object, and the canonical coproduct comparison is an isomorphism for subsets intersecting only in {∗}. Morphisms are natural isomorphisms. The Γ-space A_C([n]) = N Sum_C([n]) is special, with A_C([1]) equivalent to N(Core C), not NC. Apply the Γ-space delooping functor B of H.4/segal-delooping-theorem repeatedly to A_C; the first loop comparison group-completes |N(Core C)|, and subsequent comparisons are weak equivalences. Replacing the zeroth level by that group completion gives a connective Ω-spectrum. Categorical iteration of Sum_C is not available with these morphisms. For finite pointed sets the associated spectrum is the sphere (quoted Barratt–Priddy–Quillen–Segal); for finitely generated projective modules it is the connective K-theory spectrum. The component monoid before completion is the monoid of isomorphism classes of C under categorical sums, with the zero object as unit. The component group of the group-completed zeroth space Ω|B A_C([1])| is its algebraic Grothendieck group; the comparison sends the component of each object to its Grothendieck generator. For projective modules the operation is direct sum.
hypotheses: C has a zero object and categorical sums, and functors preserve them; symmetric monoidal categories without categorical sums (such as iso P(R)) use H.4/coherent-subset-construction instead.
Carlsson prints the range 'n > 1'; the delooping for n ≥ 1 is Segal's Proposition 1.4 (Bhatt–Scholze Proposition 12.10), recorded in H.4/segal-delooping-theorem.
proofSteps: Sum_C(f)(φ)(S) = φ(f⁻¹(S)) makes Sum_C a functor Fin_* → CAT (Carlsson §1.2).

Proposition 2: Sum_C([0]) is the contractible category of zero objects; Sum_C(n) → ∏ Sum_C(1) is an equivalence with inverse θ(φ₁, …, φ_n)({i₁, …, i_s}) = φ_{i₁}(1) ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ φ_{i_s}(1) (proof given), so Sp₁(C) is special (H.1/adjunction-homotopy-equivalence).

Evaluation at the singleton nonbasepoint is an equivalence Sum_C([1]) ≌ Core C: a summing functor is determined up to natural isomorphism by that object and its zero-object value. Iteration is instead by the Γ-space construction B, whose positive deloopings are connected and special; use H.4/segal-delooping-theorem, not categorical coproducts in Sum_C(X).
The delooping statements are H.4/segal-delooping-theorem; the group-completion statement for σ₀ is H.4/segal-group-completion-homology.

Identify the original component monoid with isomorphism classes of C, using Sum_C([1]) ≌ Core C. Apply the Γ-space group-completion comparison and the existing algebraic Grothendieck-group universal property to the completed zeroth space. Keep this map separate from the original component identification; an equivalence of small models of projective modules preserves zero objects and sums through their universal properties.
acceptance: For an abelian group A the bar construction B^n.A gives the Eilenberg–Mac Lane spectrum, a case not induced by categorical sums (Carlsson §1.2 and p. 9).
